source.versionTitle: Atra-ḫasīs, Tablet I — best-effort reconstruction from named scholarly editions
source.verificationStatus: best-effort-reconstruction-pending-verification. Reconstructed from the standard scholarly editions (Lambert & Millard 1969, the critical edition; George & Al-Rawi 1996 for the Old Babylonian Sippar witnesses; Foster 2005 Before the Muses 3rd ed.). Line numbering follows Lambert–Millard 1969. The eBL corpus L.1.1 (ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/1) and SEAL served as a collation aid only (CC BY-NC — not reproduced). The sign-by-sign transliteration is a best-effort reconstruction and is PENDING COLLATION against Lambert–Millard 1969 and eBL L.1.1; per-line sign values may contain reconstruction errors. The sense of each line is well-attested across the cited editions and should match the downstream English faithfully. This draft curates the labor-frame (I:1–71) and the creation core (I:189–276); many intervening lines are not reconstructed here and are marked by editorial-selection gap notes.

citations: Lambert, W. G., & Millard, A. R., Atra-ḫasīs: The Babylonian Story of the Flood (Oxford 1969) — the standard critical edition; line-numbering authority for this text.
George, A. R., & Al-Rawi, F. N. H., 'Tablets from the Sippar Library VI: Atra-ḫasīs,' Iraq 58 (1996), pp. 147–190 — the Old Babylonian Sippar witnesses.
Foster, B. R., Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature, 3rd ed. (Bethesda 2005), pp. 227–280 — the accessible English translation ('Atrahasis' / 'When the gods were man').
electronic Babylonian Library (eBL), corpus L.1.1, ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/1 — consulted as a collation aid only (CC BY-NC; not reproduced).
Sources of Early Akkadian Literature (SEAL) — consulted as a collation aid only.
Kilmer, A. D., 'The Mesopotamian Concept of Overpopulation and Its Solution as Reflected in the Mythology,' Orientalia 41 (1972) — for the labor/overpopulation frame.
Bottéro, J., & Kramer, S. N., Lorsque les dieux faisaient l'homme (Paris 1989), pp. 526–564 — French edition and commentary.
source.fragmentationNote: Atra-ḫasīs is a three-tablet Old Babylonian epic (c. 1700 BCE), best preserved in the copy of the scribe Ku-Aya / Ipiq-Aya (reign of Ammi-ṣaduqa). Tablet I runs to c. 416 lines in the Lambert–Millard 1969 edition and covers the primeval order of the gods, the corvée-labor of the Igigi, the night rebellion, the divine council, and the creation of humankind from clay mixed with the flesh and blood of a slaughtered god. This source file reconstructs the labor-frame (I:1–71) and the creation core (I:189–276) — the passages most on-thesis for the Wheel of Heaven program (humankind fashioned to bear the *dullu* / labor of the gods). Intervening spans not reconstructed here are flagged with editorial-selection gap notes in each segment. This is a MOAT TEXT: no usable public-domain English translation of Atra-ḫasīs exists, so the Wheel of Heaven program renders its own English from the Akkadian.

segments.label: The frame — the gods bear the labor (Lambert–Millard I:1–6)

notes: The celebrated opening of the poem, from which the standard title *inūma ilū awīlum* is drawn. *awīlum* here is read by Lambert–Millard as a comparative — the gods themselves, before humankind, doing what men would later do. The syntax is disputed (see editorial questions).
*dullu* 'labor/toil' (glossary), *šupšikku* 'earth-carrying / labor-basket' (the corvée-basket).
*šupšik ilī* 'the toil-basket of the gods.'
*dullu kabit* 'the toil was heavy'; *šapšāqu* 'hardship, distress.'
*sibittam* 'the Seven' — the seven great Anunnaki who assign the labor. *Anunnaku/Anunnaki* per glossary.
The junior Igigi-gods bear the corvée for the senior Anunnaki — the frame that motivates the whole poem.

segments.label: The great gods divide the cosmos (Lambert–Millard I:7–16)

notes: Anu, sky-god, head of the pantheon.
Enlil, the executive power, lord of the earth.
*guzalû* 'throne-bearer / chamberlain.'
*rābiṣu* 'bailiff / sheriff'; Ennugi, canal-inspector of the underworld.
*isqu nadû* 'to cast the lot' — the gods divide the cosmos by lot.
Division of cosmic spheres among the great gods.
Anu takes the sky.
Enlil takes the earth; restoration after Lambert–Millard.
The sea-lock is assigned to Enki (Ea).
Enki (Ea) receives the Apsû, the subterranean fresh water.

segments.label: The Igigi dig the Tigris, the Euphrates, and the Apsû (Lambert–Millard I:21–33, selective)

preceding_lacuna.text: Intervening lines I:17–20 (the descent of Enki to the Apsû, transition to the Igigi's toil) are not reconstructed in this draft.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: lines I:17–20 are not reconstructed in this draft, which curates the labor-frame and the creation core.]

notes: *ḫerû* 'to dig'; *nāru* 'river.' The Igigi excavate the great watercourses of Mesopotamia.
The Euphrates dug 'second' (ša-ni-tam).
*naqbu* 'underground water-source, deep'; *būru* 'cistern / spring.'
*apsû* — the subterranean fresh-water abyss, Enki's domain.

segments.label: The years of toil and the night rebellion (Lambert–Millard I:37–71, selective)

preceding_lacuna.text: Intervening lines I:26–36 (the counting of the years of toil) are compressed; the draft resumes at the tally of years and the grumbling.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: lines I:26–36 are compressed in this draft.]

notes: The number of years is damaged and disputed — variously read as forty or 3600 (see editorial questions).
The toil is unremitting.
*nazāmu* 'to grumble, complain'; *kalakku* 'excavation, diggings.'
The Igigi collectively voice their grievance.
The rebel resolve; *tāḫāzu* 'battle.' The Igigi determine to confront Enlil.
*išātu* 'fire'; *unūtu* 'equipment, tools.' The burning of the labor-implements.
*allu* 'hoe / spade'; *qâlu* (Š) 'to set alight.'
The corvée-baskets themselves are burnt — the symbolic renunciation of the labor.
The night march on Enlil's temple, the Ekur.
*saḫāru* 'to surround'; the Ekur, Enlil's temple at Nippur, is besieged.

segments.label: The council of Anu, Enlil, and Enki (Lambert–Millard I:72–170, selective)

preceding_lacuna.text: The council scene (Nusku rousing Enlil, Enlil's fright and tears, the summoning of Anu and Enki, the deadlock over the ringleader) is reconstructed only in outline here; many lines I:72–169 are not reproduced in this draft.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: the council dialogue I:72–169 is given only in outline in this draft.]

notes: *Nusku*, Enlil's vizier; *dekû* 'to rouse.'
Enlil weeps in fright at the surrounded temple; *dimtu* 'tear.'
Anu descends to the council; sequence approximate.
Enki (Ea) joins the divine assembly.
The council interrogates the cause of the revolt; *bānû qabli* 'maker of the conflict.'
The Igigi answer as one body: the toil itself, not a single ringleader, is intolerable. The deadlock that motivates Ea's proposal.

segments.label: Enki's plan — the creation of the lullû to bear the labor (Lambert–Millard I:189–199)

preceding_lacuna.text: Lines I:170–188 (the transition from the deadlock to Enki's address) are not reconstructed in this draft; the creation core resumes at Enki's proposal.

i18n.en: [Editorial selection: lines I:170–188 are not reconstructed in this draft.]

notes: Speech-introduction formula; Enki (Ea) addresses the assembly.
*izakkar ana ilī rabûtim* 'he spoke to the great gods.'
*Bēlet-ilī* 'Mistress-of-the-gods,' the birth-goddess (epithet-cluster per glossary); *šassūru* 'womb, womb-goddess.'
*lullû* — the newly-fashioned primeval human (see editorial questions); *banû* 'to create, fashion.'
*abšānu* 'yoke, harness' — the labor-yoke transferred to humankind.
*šipru* 'work, task'; the labor formerly borne by the Igigi.
*awīlum lišši dulli ilī* 'let man carry the toil of the gods' — the thesis-line of Mesopotamian anthropogony. *dullu* per glossary; *awīlum* flagged.
The assembly calls the birth-goddess.
*mūdâ* 'the knowing/wise one.'
*bāniat awīlūti* 'she who creates humankind'; *awīlūtu* 'humanity.'
*nīru* 'yoke' (synonym of *abšānu*); *lullû* flagged.

segments.label: The slaughter of Wê-ila and the mixing of flesh, blood, and clay (Lambert–Millard I:200–229)

notes: *Nintu* (= Bēlet-ilī / Mami), the birth-goddess (epithet-cluster per glossary).
Speech-introduction.
*lā nāṭu* 'it is not fitting'; Nintu cannot act without Enki's purifying power.
*šiprum* 'the work'; the craft is Enki's.
*elēlu* (D) 'to purify'; Enki's purification enables the creation.
*ṭiṭṭu* 'clay' (glossary, substance-cognate cluster); the raw material of humankind.
Speech-introduction.
Speech-introduction.

lines.translit: i-na wa-ar-ḫi-im u4-1-kam u4-7-kam ù u4-15-kam
notes: The purification-days of the lunar month.
*tēliltu* 'purification'; *rimku* 'ablution-bath.'
*ṭabāḫu* 'to slaughter (ritually).' A single god is put to death to supply the divine element in humanity.
*ṭebû/ṭabāḫu* — the gods purified through the slain god's immolation.
*šīru* 'flesh' + *damu* 'blood' — the divine substances (see editorial questions on the triad).
*balālu* 'to mix'; flesh and blood kneaded into *ṭiṭṭu* 'clay' (glossary).
*ilumma u awīlum* 'god and man together' — the compound nature of the human being. *awīlum* flagged.
The god and the human commingled in the clay-matrix.

lines.translit: a-na du-úr da-ar up-pa i ni-iš-me
notes: *uppu* — variously 'drum,' or the heartbeat/pulse, or a token of the ghost's presence (see editorial questions).
*eṭemmu* 'ghost, spirit' — the enduring divine element in the human (see editorial questions).
*balṭu* 'the living (one)'; *ittu* 'sign, token'; *(w)edû* (Š) 'to make known.'
*mušši* 'forgetting'; the *eṭemmu* is the guarantor of remembrance beyond death.
*annu apālu* 'to answer yes, to assent'; *puḫru* 'assembly.'
*mušīmū šīmātim* 'the fate-decreers' — the great gods; *Anunna(ki)* per glossary.

lines.translit: il-qú-ú-ma we-e i-la ša i-šu-ú ṭe4-e-ma
notes: *Wê-ila* — the slaughtered god (reading contested); *ṭēmu* 'reason, intelligence, planning-capacity' (both flagged in editorial questions). The pun *Wê + ila + ṭēmu → awīlu + eṭemmu* is the etymological heart of the passage.
The ritual killing of the god carried out.
*šīru* + *damu* again — now the act, not the plan.
The birth-goddess kneads the divine flesh and blood into the clay.
Fulfilment of the wish at I:216; *uppu* crux (see editorial questions).
The *eṭemmu* now exists — the human being carries the ghost of the slain god.
The ghost proclaims itself to the living.
Closure of the eṭemmu-etiology.

segments.label: The Igigi spit on the clay; Mami's speech (Lambert–Millard I:230–248)

notes: *ištu balālu ṭiṭṭa* 'once she had blended the clay.'
The great gods called to witness.
The junior gods now participate in the creation.
*ruʾtu* 'spittle'; *malû* 'to fill, cover.' The Igigi's saliva animates or ratifies the clay.
*Mami* — another epithet of the birth-goddess (glossary cluster).
Speech-introduction.
*šipru* 'work, commission.'
*šuklulu* 'to bring to completion.'
*qadu ṭēmišu* 'along with his intelligence' — the divine reason enters humanity; *ṭēmu* flagged.
*dullu kabtu* 'the heavy toil'; *nasāku* (Š) 'to take away.' The relief of the gods accomplished.
*tupšikku* 'labor-basket'; *emēdu* 'to impose.' The corvée transferred to humankind; *awīlu* flagged.
*rigmu* 'noise, clamor' — the human din that will later provoke the flood; *awīlūtu* 'humankind.'
*paṭāru* 'to loosen'; *abšānu* 'yoke'; *urûtu* uncertain — 'freedom' or 'the (birthing-)stool' (reading disputed).

segments.label: The fourteen pieces of clay — seven male, seven female (Lambert–Millard I:249–276, selective)

notes: The gods respond to Mami's declaration.
*našāqu šēpī* 'to kiss the feet' — homage to the birth-goddess.
The renaming of the goddess in honor of her deed.

lines.translit: i-na-an-na be-le-et ka-la i-li lu šu-um-ki
notes: *Bēlet-kala-ilī* 'Mistress-of-all-the-gods' — the new honorific.
*bīt šīmti* 'house of fate' — the birthing chamber where destinies are fixed.
Enki and Nintu together conduct the creation.
*šassūrātu* — the birth-goddesses in the plural, the assisting midwives.
*kabāsu* 'to tread, knead'; Enki treads the clay before Nintu.
*šiptu* 'incantation'; the spell that accompanies the fashioning.
Enki dictates the incantation to Nintu; *šudbubu* 'to cause to recite.'
*gamāru* 'to complete.'
*karāṣu* 'to pinch off'; *kiṣru* 'lump, piece.' The fourteen portions of the clay.
*imittu* 'right side' — the male portions.
*šumēlu* 'left side' — the female portions.
*libittu* — the birth-brick on which the mother squats; here the divider between male and female lumps.
The seven-and-seven midwife-goddesses.
*banû* 'to fashion'; *zikaru* 'male.'
*sinništu* 'female.' The primal seven pairs of humankind.
*bāniat šīmti* 'she who creates fate.'
The pairs finished off in couples.
*uṣurāt nišī* 'the designs/forms of the people'; *eṣēru* 'to draw, design.' Humankind patterned by the birth-goddess.
